summary_html: A **child is removed without exigency or warrant**, violating constitutional rights. Federal courts treat such removals as seizures under the Fourth and Fourteenth Amendments, actionable via §1983.
authority_html:
- **ASFA / SSA Title IV-E** — limits removals to lawful emergencies and requires judicial review  
- **U.S. Constitution (4th & 14th Amendments)** — protects family integrity; requires due process

case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit
key_cases.holding: In an Oregon case, the court held that the in-school seizure and interview of a child by a caseworker and deputy without a warrant, court order, exigency or parental consent violated the Fourth Amendment (though those defendants had qualified immunity), and that the subsequent removal and medical examination also violated the family's rights.
key_cases.relevance: Addresses the removal and compelled medical examination that followed the interview as separate constitutional violations.
key_cases.quote: we hold that the investigation conducted by Camreta and Alford and the removal and examination instigated by Camreta all violated Sarah and the girls' constitutional rights

key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit
key_cases.holding: In an Oregon case, the court held city police officers who assisted an ORS 419B.150 removal at the direction of Oregon DHS were entitled to qualified immunity because their reliance on the agency's protective-custody determination was objectively reasonable.
key_cases.relevance: Identifies who can and cannot be held liable under § 1983 for an Oregon removal later shown to be unjustified.
key_cases.quote: Sjurset correctly points out, however, that an officer cannot blindly rely on the existence of a protective-custody determination to avoid liability.

key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit
key_cases.holding: Sitting en banc, the court held a genuine dispute existed as to whether a newborn was in imminent danger justifying warrantless removal, because social workers may not forgo a warrant if they had adequate time to obtain one without risking the child.
key_cases.relevance: Provides the current framework for § 1983 warrantless-removal liability binding on Oregon agencies.
key_cases.quote: under Rogers, the social workers here lacked cause to forgo a warrant if they had adequate time to pursue one through the ordinary judicial process

key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit
key_cases.holding: The court held that a social worker and police officer were not entitled to qualified immunity for a coerced warrantless entry into a home to investigate suspected child abuse, or for the strip search of a three-year-old, because the Fourth Amendment applies to child-abuse investigations.
key_cases.relevance: The leading Ninth Circuit authority that there is no child-welfare exception to the Fourth Amendment's warrant requirement for home entry.
key_cases.quote: It does not hold that the social worker may enter the home despite the absence of consent or exigency.

key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit
key_cases.holding: The court held a social worker was not entitled to summary judgment on a warrantless-seizure claim because officials must obtain prior judicial authorization before removing a child absent reasonable cause to believe the child faces imminent danger of serious bodily injury.
key_cases.relevance: Defines what makes a removal unlawful and actionable under § 1983 in this circuit.
key_cases.quote: Government officials are required to obtain prior judicial authorization before intruding on a parent's custody of her child unless they possess information at the time of the seizure

key_cases.case_name: Scanlon v. County of Los Angeles
key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit
key_cases.holding: The court held the agency's statement of cause supporting a protective custody warrant contained material misrepresentations and omissions such that a reasonable magistrate informed of the true facts would not have issued it, and remanded the judicial-deception claim.
key_cases.relevance: The most recent published Ninth Circuit authority on § 1983 liability for a removal procured by a materially false or incomplete warrant application.
key_cases.quote: We conclude that the Statement contained misrepresentations and omissions of fact and so remand to the district court.

state_agency.name: Oregon Department of Human Services, Child Welfare Division

timeline_requirements.starts_from: Entry of the juvenile court's judgment
timeline_requirements.consequence_of_miss: The notice of appeal is untimely, but ORS 419A.200(5)(a) provides that on motion of a person other than the state the appellate court shall grant leave to file a notice of appeal after the time limit if the person shows a colorable claim of error and that the failure to file timely is not personally attributable to the person; that request must be filed no later than 90 days after entry of the judgment (ORS 419A.200(5)(c)). Where the circuit court grants a rehearing on a motion made not later than 15 days after entry of judgment, the time for taking an appeal runs from entry of the judgment after the rehearing (ORS 419A.200(2)).
